title: The Potter and the Clay
summary: God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter at his wheel, reshaping a spoiled vessel into another, and teaches that he can do the same with Israel and any nation: announced judgment can be withdrawn if a people turns, and announced blessing can be withdrawn if it turns to evil. Judah refuses, declaring its case hopeless. When the people plot against him, Jeremiah prays in his fourth confession, asking God to bring on his enemies the disaster they deserve.
story: This chapter and the next form a pair built around pottery. Here the clay is still soft and can be reshaped; in chapter 19 Jeremiah will smash a hardened jar that cannot be repaired. Chapter 18 is therefore a door held open. It explains the purpose of all Jeremiah's warnings: prophecy of disaster was not fate but summons, and God's announced plans responded to how nations answered him. Judah's reply, "It is hopeless", shows what the problem really is. It is not that God will not relent but that the people will not turn. The chapter ends with the prophet under attack once more, and his prayer grows harsher than in any earlier confession.
historical:
The chapter is undated, but its setting is the same final decades of Judah's kingdom, probably in the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC), when Jeremiah's opponents were numerous and powerful. Verse 18 shows who they were: people confident that "the law will never be lost to the priest, nor counsel to the wise, nor an oracle to the prophet". These were the three recognized sources of guidance in Judah: priests who taught the law (torah), wise men and royal counselors who gave advice, and prophets who spoke oracles. Ezekiel names the same three (Ezekiel 7:26). Jeremiah's enemies are saying that the religious establishment is secure and one troublesome prophet can be discarded without loss.

Potters were among the most common craftsmen in any ancient town. Archaeologists have found potters' workshops and kilns from the Iron Age in the land of Israel, and pottery fragments are so abundant and so characteristic of their period that they are the main tool archaeologists use to date layers at a site.
cultural:
The potter's wheel in Jeremiah's day was typically made of two stone discs, one above the other on a pivot; the Hebrew word for wheel in verse 3 has a dual ending, suggesting this pair. The potter turned the lower wheel with his feet or had an assistant turn it, and shaped the clay with his hands on the upper. If the clay had a flaw, such as a stone or an air bubble or an uneven wall, the potter could press it back into a lump and begin again while it was still wet. Once fired in the kiln, a vessel could no longer be reshaped, only broken.

The snow of Lebanon (verse 14) refers to the high peaks of the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, including Mount Hermon, which hold snow for much of the year and feed cold springs and streams below. Jeremiah contrasts their reliability with Israel's fickleness: even nature keeps faith better than God's people. Whistling or hissing at a ruined place and shaking the head (verse 16) were gestures of shock and scorn at another's disaster. The "ancient roads" of verse 15 are the long-established paths of Israel's faith, contrasted with rough byways that lead nowhere.
literary: The chapter opens with a report of a sign that Jeremiah observes rather than performs (verses 1 to 4), followed by its interpretation (verses 5 to 12). The interpretation lays out two parallel cases (verses 7 and 8, verses 9 and 10), each built on the same verbs as Jeremiah's call in 1:10: uproot, tear down, destroy, build, plant. The Hebrew uses a pun running through the chapter: the potter (yotser) forms clay, and God in verse 11 is "planning" (yotser, the same verb) a disaster, shaping it as a potter shapes a pot. A poem of lament over Israel's unnatural forgetting follows (verses 13 to 17), and the chapter ends with the fourth confession (verses 18 to 23), where the people's plot ("Come, let us make plans") meets the prophet's prayer for justice.

outline.t: Like clay in the potter's hand
Turn now, and Judah's answer: it is hopeless
Israel has forgotten me: a lament
A plot against Jeremiah and his prayer for justice

doctrines.note: God is the potter and nations are the clay. He has the right and power to shape, reshape, or discard. Yet verses 7 to 10 show that his sovereignty is not mechanical: he responds to how nations turn.
The chapter makes repentance the hinge of history. A warned nation that turns from evil finds God relenting, which is why the call "Turn now" is urgent rather than futile.
Judgment is announced in order to be averted. When Judah answers "It is hopeless", it chooses the judgment it was warned about.

words.note: Yatsar, to form or shape, and as a noun, a potter. It is the verb of Genesis 2:7, where the LORD God formed the man from the dust, and of Isaiah's reminders that Israel is clay in God's hands (Isaiah 64:8). In verse 11 the same verb is used for God "planning" a disaster, so the potter's workshop becomes a picture of God's work in history.

Nacham, to relent, be sorry, or change one's course. In verses 8 and 10 God says he will relent of the disaster or of the good he had intended. The word raises a real theological question, since elsewhere God does not change his mind like a human (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Most interpreters take the two together: God's character and purpose do not change, and that unchanging character responds differently to repentance than to rebellion, as Jonah 3:10 shows at Nineveh.

Kipper, to atone, cover, or make expiation, the key verb of Israel's sacrificial system and the Day of Atonement. In verse 23 Jeremiah uses it in the negative: do not atone for their guilt. The prophet who once interceded for his people now asks God to withhold the very mercy the sacrifices were meant to provide.

christ: Paul takes up the potter image in Romans 9:20-21, drawing on this chapter and on Isaiah (29:16; 45:9), to argue that God has the right to shape his purposes in history as he wills, including his mercy toward Gentiles. The chapter's emphasis on a God who relents when people turn is also the ground of the gospel's call to repentance: the preaching of John the Baptist and Jesus begins with the same summons, turn, because the kingdom is near (Matthew 3:2; 4:17). Jeremiah's prayer in verses 19 to 23, where he recalls how he "stood before You to speak good on their behalf" and then asks for their destruction, stands in contrast with Jesus, who also was plotted against by the religious leaders and repaid good with evil, yet prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) and taught his followers to bless those who curse them (Luke 6:28). That contrast is not a condemnation of Jeremiah but a measure of what is new in Christ.

hard.q: How can a prophet of God pray for his enemies' children to starve and their husbands to die?
hard.a: Verses 21 to 23 are among the harshest words in any prophet's mouth, and they belong to a kind of prayer called imprecation, found also in Psalms such as 69, 109, and 137. Several things help a reader. First, Jeremiah does not take revenge; he hands the case to God, the judge who knows "all their deadly plots". Second, what he asks for is the very judgment God had already announced against the city (sword, famine, and death), so he is asking God to carry out his declared justice against people trying to kill his messenger. Third, the prayer is honest: Scripture records the rage of a man betrayed after interceding for his attackers, rather than hiding it. Interpreters differ on whether to read the prayer as a model or as a faithful record of a suffering man's words that God then answers in his own way. Christians also read it in light of Jesus' command to love enemies, which does not deny the longing for justice but entrusts it wholly to God (Romans 12:19).

questions: God says he will relent when a nation turns. How does it change the way you hear warnings in Scripture to know that they are invitations as well as threats?
Judah said, "It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans." When have you been tempted to decide that change is impossible, and what did that decision protect?
Jeremiah brought his rage to God instead of acting on it. What would it look like for you to bring your anger about a real injustice to God in honest prayer?
